Delitzsch notes that the Psalter closes with five Hallelujah psalms, this first having so many points of contact with the alphabetical hymn before it that the same range of thought betrays one author. In the Greek these psalms carry the inscription of Haggai and Zechariah, repeated four times, which suggests a separate Hallel referred back to those prophets in the liturgy of the second Temple. Clarke reports the same evidence — no name in the Hebrew or Chaldee, but those two prophets in the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic — and dates it after the captivity, to the moment when Cyrus withdrew his order for rebuilding the walls. That would give verse 3 its edge. Calvin knows the same facts and Horsley's title, a thanksgiving of the returning captives, but sees nothing forbidding us to take the psalm for David's.

Henry reads it as David's, and finds the point in the speaker. David was a prince, and it might be thought enough that his priests and people praised God without his doing it in person — Michal thought it a disparagement to him to dance before the ark — but he judged his dignity obliged him to lead. Then the other half: having been so great a blessing to his country, he might have been adored as the heathen deified their heroes. Put not your trust in princes, he answers — not in me, not in any. Some have thought they knew better how to reign by knowing how to dissemble; and the honest are sons of Adam, weak and mortal, so that a king's power may be too cramped for what is expected of him — as David owned in calling himself that day weak, though anointed king. Gill adds that princes are called benefactors for their bounty and are fickle nonetheless: men of high degree are a lie.

Calvin takes the psalm's subject to be the diseased disposition, almost universally prevalent, of deceiving ourselves with expectations from every quarter, and its remedy a hope centred wholly in God. On the address to his own soul he observes that the impulse was not volatile and superficial but a staid affection proved by its effects not to be feigned, applied to his own zeal before he set up as anyone's teacher. Spurgeon says it more sharply. It is poor business to exhort others without stirring one's own soul, an evil thing to say Praise ye and never add Praise, O my soul; and he pulls himself up mid-exhortation to ask what he is at, calling on others while negligent. He also grieves that Hallelujah has been trailed in the mire of late, blaming the leaders who countenance it rather than the ruder sort who use it ignorantly.

Augustine asks the harder question: who says it, and to whom? Not the flesh giving counsel to the soul, for the body is beneath the soul, and any soul, however vile, is more excellent than the most excellent body — not in deserts but in nature, as gold, though rusted, is better than polished lead. The voice encouraging its own soul, he tells his hearers, is theirs if they will.

On the last verse the commentators go small. Clarke hangs a man's existence on the air he breathes: when he ceases to respire, his body claims its affinity to the earth and all his projects come to nothing. Wesley glosses that day as soon as he is dead, the thoughts as all his designs. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew for thoughts occurs nowhere else and would be rendered etymologically by fabrications, and sets Antony beside it — but yesterday the word of Caesar might have stood against the world, and now none so poor to do him reverence. On verse 2 Clarke found the opposite word as expressive: while I have any being means in my continuance, my progression, my eternal existence.
5:
Three commentators notice the same thing about verses 7 to 9, and none notices the others. Delitzsch counts five lines each beginning with the divine name and each of exactly three words, the brevity being the favourite measure of Job; Ellicott counts the same five lines, the same three words, the same rhythm prominent in Job; Henry counts the name of Jehovah five times in five lines and reads the repetition as intimating an almighty power engaged for the oppressed — it being as much God's glory to succour those in misery as to ride upon the heavens. Delitzsch adds that the five lines celebrate the God of the five-divisioned Law, directed with particular tenderness toward strangers, orphans and widows, and quotes Bakius, who found the psalm dear for that Trefoil of God set out in one verse as nowhere else in the Psalter.

Two words in the catalogue Ellicott corrects. To relieve the fatherless and widow is rather to restore them by taking up their cause — some forms of the verb bear witness, so a court may be in view, with God testifying for the defenceless. And to turn the way of the wicked upside down is rather to bend it aside: the same word elsewhere is rendered dealt perversely, the idea being interference — when the wicked man has laid out his plans and looks along a level road, providence bends the course and makes the path crooked. Clarke reaches much the same sense by another route: they shall not do all the wickedness they wish, but be stopped, turned aside, or overturned. Wesley, on the faithfulness kept for ever, gives two reasons: God lives for ever to fulfil his promises, and is eternally faithful.

Where the blindness of verse 8 belongs is the one real dispute. Ellicott allows both senses — distress, or want of spiritual discernment — and decides for the former. Gill takes the whole catalogue for a description of Christ: the eyes opened are those of the men he healed and of one born blind, and, spiritually, of anyone brought to see his own danger through the word preached; the strangers preserved include the Syrophenician woman and the Samaritan. Henry wants both, citing Hammond, who read the psalm's latter part as looking toward the incarnate Son and quoted a rabbi holding verse 10 to belong to the Messiah's days. His own evidence is that the characters here are those Christ gave John's disciples — the blind receive their sight, the lame walk — and that the beatitude on the man not offended in him answers verse 5.

Clarke keeps the historical line to the end and makes it pastoral. In the son of man there is no saving principle, and this son of Adam returns to the ground he came from; but the God who helped Jacob does not change and has purposed that Israel shall be delivered. Cyrus may change his mind; God will not. He has preserved you as strangers in a strange land for seventy years, provided for the widow and fatherless as fully as in the promised land, and sustained you so long that he will bring you out. Fear not.

Henry's catalogue runs alongside, each mercy answered by an instance: food given the hungry when ravens fed Elijah; prisoners loosed out of Egypt and Babylon; the eyes of the blind opened, since it was not heard since the world began that any man opened the eyes of one born blind; the bowed down raised, as the woman was made straight who could in no wise lift up herself. Gill ends where the psalm does, with a reign that outlasts the princes of verse 3 — they reign a while, he for evermore — noting that Jarchi and Kimchi refer the verse to the Messiah's kingdom. Ellicott's whole note there is a cross-reference to the song at the sea.
